thesis.label: Thesis
thesis.title: How to make your thesis
thesis.intro: Ten stages, from choosing a topic to final submission.

paper.label: Research Paper
paper.title: How to make your research paper
paper.intro: Ten stages, from selecting a problem to responding to reviewers.

guides.title: How to choose a research topic
guides.description: Move from a broad interest to a focused, feasible research topic you can finish.
guides.intro: A topic is not a subject area. It is a specific, answerable question inside one.
guides.whatIsIt: A research topic names the narrow question your study will answer. “Employee motivation” is a subject area; “how hybrid work arrangements affect intrinsic motivation among IT professionals in one metropolitan region” is a topic.
guides.whyItMatters: Topic selection constrains every later decision: your literature, method, sample and timeline. A topic chosen carelessly cannot be rescued by good writing later.

howTo.text: You will live with this for months. Interest sustains the boring middle stretch.
Add a population, setting, time frame or variable until the question is answerable within your registration period.

howTo.step: Read recent issues of your target journals
howTo.text: Live debate shows where the field is still arguing. Silence usually means the question is settled, or nobody considers it important.
Write one sentence: we do not yet know X, because prior work has only done Y. If you cannot write it, keep reading.
Access, permission, sample size, cost, instruments, supervisor expertise. A brilliant question with unreachable data is not a topic.
Name the variables, the population and the context. Expect to revise it once the literature review is done.

examples.strong: Example only: the effect of hybrid work arrangements on intrinsic motivation among IT professionals in one metropolitan region, over a defined two-year period.
examples.weak: Example only: a study on employee motivation.

mistakes: Committing to a topic before checking whether the data is reachable
Choosing a question so broad that no single study could answer it
Picking an area with no live debate in recent literature
Ignoring whether your supervisor can actually supervise it
checklist: My topic names a population, a context and a variable or phenomenon
I can state the gap in one sentence
I know where the data will come from and that I can obtain it
The scope fits my registration period
My supervisor has relevant expertise
guides.takeaway: A good topic is the most finishable one, not the most interesting one.
guides.seoTitle: How to choose a research topic
guides.metaDescription: Move from a broad interest to a focused, feasible research topic you can finish.

guides.title: How to define a research problem
guides.description: Turn a topic into a stated problem supported by evidence from the literature.
guides.intro: A topic tells a reader what you are studying. A research problem tells them why it needs studying.
guides.whatIsIt: A research problem is a documented gap or tension: something the field does not know, or where published accounts disagree, stated with evidence rather than asserted.
guides.whyItMatters: Examiners and reviewers test whether the problem is real. “Limited research exists” is a claim; a problem built on what the literature actually shows is a finding.

howTo.text: Establish the context a reader needs before the problem can make sense.
Cite what prior studies found, and show precisely where they stop.
Contradictory findings, an untested population, an unexamined context, or a method never applied in this setting.
One paragraph: what is unknown, why it matters, and what your study addresses.
Say plainly what the study does not cover. Scope stated by you is rigour; scope found by an examiner is a weakness.

examples.strong: Example only: prior studies report higher autonomy under hybrid arrangements but conflicting effects on motivation, and none separates voluntary from mandated arrangements — which may explain the divergence.
examples.weak: Example only: there is limited research on hybrid work and motivation.

mistakes: Asserting a gap instead of demonstrating it
Describing a topic and calling it a problem
Writing a problem so large that no study could address it
Leaving scope undefined, so the study appears to over-claim
checklist: My problem is supported by cited evidence, not assertion
The gap is specific, not “more research is needed”
A reader can see why this matters
Scope and delimitations are stated
The problem is answerable with my available method and data
guides.takeaway: A problem you can evidence is worth more than one that merely sounds important.
guides.seoTitle: How to define a research problem
guides.metaDescription: Turn a topic into a stated problem supported by evidence from the literature.

guides.title: How to write research objectives and questions
guides.description: Write an aim, objectives and questions that align with each other and with your method.
guides.intro: The aim is the destination. Objectives are the stages. Research questions are what you will actually answer.
guides.whatIsIt: An aim states the overall purpose in one sentence. Objectives break it into achievable components, usually three to five. Research questions restate objectives in answerable form; hypotheses do so only where the design is testable.
guides.whyItMatters: Misalignment here surfaces everywhere later: an objective with no matching method, a question your data cannot answer, a finding that answers nothing you asked. Examiners check this chain first.

howTo.text: One sentence, beginning “this study aims to…”
Three to five, each starting with a verb you can actually perform: examine, compare, assess, determine.
Each objective becomes one answerable question. One-to-one, with no orphans on either side.
Testable designs need them; exploratory and most qualitative work does not.
Tabulate objective → question → data source → analysis. Every row must be complete before you collect anything.

examples.strong: Example only — objective: to compare intrinsic motivation between hybrid and on-site professionals. Question: does intrinsic motivation differ between the two groups?
examples.weak: Example only — objective: to study hybrid work. Question: what is hybrid work?

mistakes: Objectives using unmeasurable verbs with no method attached
More questions than objectives, or questions no objective covers
Hypotheses added to a qualitative study because a template demanded them
Objectives written after the data was collected
checklist: I have one aim, in one sentence
Every objective starts with a performable verb
Each objective maps to exactly one research question
Every question maps to a data source and an analysis
Hypotheses appear only where the design tests them
guides.takeaway: If you cannot tabulate objective → question → method → analysis, the chain is broken somewhere.
guides.seoTitle: How to write research objectives and questions
guides.metaDescription: Write an aim, objectives and questions that align with each other and with your method.

guides.title: How to conduct a literature review
guides.description: Build an argument from prior work rather than a catalogue of summaries.
guides.intro: A literature review is an argument about a field, not a list of what people said.
guides.whatIsIt: A review synthesises prior work: what is established, where accounts disagree, and what remains unanswered. It ends by making your research question feel inevitable.
guides.whyItMatters: “Descriptive rather than critical” is the most common examiner comment on a review. It usually means the chapter is organised by author instead of by idea.

howTo.text: Databases, keywords, date range, inclusion and exclusion criteria. Record it — examiners ask.

howTo.step: Read for position, not just content
howTo.text: Note what each study claims, on what evidence, and where it stops.
When subheadings are concepts rather than names, the writing turns critical almost on its own.
Studies that disagree with your position are the most useful ones you have.
The gap should emerge from the evidence you just presented, not appear as an assertion.

Record every source at the moment you use it. Reconstructing citations later is where accidental plagiarism enters. Summarise in your own words and cite; never reuse sentence structure with words swapped.

examples.strong: Example only: three studies report higher autonomy; two report reduced cohesion. None separates voluntary from mandated arrangements, which may explain the divergence.
examples.weak: Example only: Author A said this. Author B said that. Author C said both.

mistakes: Summarising study by study instead of comparing
No stated search strategy or inclusion criteria
Omitting studies that contradict your expected finding
Paraphrasing so closely that the wording remains the source's
checklist: I can state my search strategy in three sentences
My subheadings are themes, not author names
Contradictory findings are addressed, not hidden
Every claim carries a citation
The chapter ends by making my question feel necessary
guides.takeaway: Organise by idea, not by author, and the review becomes critical on its own.
guides.seoTitle: How to conduct a literature review
guides.metaDescription: Build an argument from prior work rather than a catalogue of summaries.

guides.title: How to write research methodology
guides.description: Justify a design your examiners can follow, repeat and defend.
guides.intro: Methodology explains how the study was done, in enough detail that someone else could repeat it.
guides.whatIsIt: The chapter states design, approach, population and sample, data sources, instruments, collection procedure, analysis and ethical clearance — each with a reason, not just a description.
guides.whyItMatters: This is the chapter examiners scrutinise most closely, because every later claim rests on it. A description without justification cannot be defended in a viva.

howTo.step: Choose a design that fits the question
howTo.text: The question decides the method, never the reverse. There is no universally correct methodology; it depends on your question and your discipline.
Quantitative, qualitative or mixed — and why that serves this question.
Sampling technique, size, and the justification for that size.
Source or development, validity and reliability evidence, and pilot testing.
Procedure, consent, approval, anonymisation and data handling.
Name the techniques, and check their assumptions before you rely on them.
A limitation you name is rigour. The same one found by an examiner is a weakness.

examples.strong: Example only: a cross-sectional design was chosen because the objective compares two existing groups at one point in time; stratified sampling ensured proportional representation of both arrangements.
examples.weak: Example only: a survey method was used. The sample was 200 respondents.

mistakes: Describing the method without justifying it
Writing methodology after collecting data, so the design cannot be defended
Reporting a sample size with no basis
Applying a statistical test without checking its assumptions
checklist: Every choice has a stated reason
Sample size is justified, not merely reported
Instrument validity and reliability are evidenced
Ethical approval and consent are documented
Analysis matches each hypothesis or question
guides.takeaway: Methodology follows the question. If you chose the method first, expect to defend the wrong thing.
guides.seoTitle: How to write research methodology
guides.metaDescription: Justify a design your examiners can follow, repeat and defend.

guides.title: How to collect and analyse research data
guides.description: Prepare, analyse and interpret data transparently, whatever your discipline.
guides.intro: Analysis turns collected data into evidence. It does not turn weak evidence into strong claims.
guides.whatIsIt: Data work covers collection, preparation, cleaning, coding, analysis and interpretation. Quantitative and qualitative traditions differ in technique but share the same obligation to transparency.
guides.whyItMatters: Most analysis problems are preparation problems: uncleaned data, undocumented exclusions, coding decisions made silently. Record every decision as you make it.

howTo.text: Handle missing values, outliers and inconsistencies — and record what you did and why.
Primary data you collected; secondary data someone else did. Each carries different limitations, and both must be described.
Quantitative: a documented codebook. Qualitative: an auditable coding frame someone else could follow.
A test run on violated assumptions produces a number, not a finding.
If you change technique, say so and say why. Never run tests repeatedly until one reaches significance.
Report what the data shows. Correlation is not causation, and a non-significant result is a result, not a failure.

examples.strong: Example only: of the responses received, a number were excluded for incomplete scales; the exclusions and the missing-data approach are reported in the analysis chapter.
examples.weak: Example only: data was analysed and the results were significant.

mistakes: Running tests repeatedly until one reaches significance
Excluding cases without reporting the exclusions
Presenting correlation as causation
Altering or selectively reporting data to fit an expected result
checklist: Cleaning and exclusions are documented
Assumptions were checked before testing
The analysis matches what the methodology promised
Tables and figures stand on their own
No claim exceeds what the data supports
guides.takeaway: Document every decision as you make it. Reconstructed analysis is never fully defensible.
guides.seoTitle: How to collect and analyse research data
guides.metaDescription: Prepare, analyse and interpret data transparently, whatever your discipline.

guides.title: How to write results and discussion
guides.description: Separate what you found from what it means — the distinction examiners look for first.
guides.intro: Results report. Discussion interprets. Collapsing the two is the most common structural fault in a thesis.
guides.whatIsIt: The results chapter presents findings neutrally and in an organised way. The discussion explains them against your objectives, your framework and prior studies.
guides.whyItMatters: A discussion that restates the results table has done no work. One that explains why a finding agrees with some prior studies and contradicts others is doing exactly what the chapter is for.

howTo.text: Organise by objective or question. No interpretation, no speculation.

howTo.step: Open the discussion with the answer
howTo.text: Address each objective directly before elaborating.
Agreement and disagreement both matter. Explain the disagreement rather than omitting it.
Show how findings support, extend or complicate the theory you used.
An unexplained result is a weakness; an examined one is a contribution.
Theoretical and practical, bounded by what your design can actually support.

examples.strong: Example only: motivation was higher in one group. This aligns with autonomy-based accounts but contradicts studies reporting cohesion loss, possibly because participation here was voluntary.
examples.weak: Example only: the results show this approach is better, which proves the hypothesis.

mistakes: Repeating the results table in prose and calling it discussion
Interpreting inside the results chapter
Ignoring findings that contradict expectations
Claiming proof from a single study
checklist: Results contain no interpretation
Every objective is answered explicitly in the discussion
Agreements and disagreements with prior work are both addressed
Unexpected findings are examined
Implications stay within what the design supports
guides.takeaway: If your discussion could be deleted without losing meaning, it was a second results chapter.
guides.seoTitle: How to write results and discussion
guides.metaDescription: Separate what you found from what it means — the distinction examiners look for first.

guides.title: How to write a conclusion and recommendations
guides.description: Close the study honestly: findings, contribution, limitations and what comes next.
guides.intro: The conclusion is where you say what the study established, and what it did not.
guides.whatIsIt: A conclusion summarises major findings, states the contribution, draws implications, acknowledges limitations and points to future research. It introduces nothing new.
guides.whyItMatters: Readers often read the introduction and the conclusion only. This chapter should be comprehensible on its own, without over-claiming.

howTo.text: Against the objectives, briefly. No new data, no new citations.
What does the field now know that it did not before your study?
Theoretical, practical or policy — only those your evidence supports.
Design, sample, context, instrument. Naming them strengthens the work.
Specific next steps that follow from your limitations, not a generic call for more research.

examples.strong: Example only: findings are limited to voluntary arrangements in one sector; whether they hold under mandated policies remains open.
examples.weak: Example only: this study proves the approach increases motivation in all organisations.

mistakes: Introducing new findings or citations in the conclusion
Generalising far beyond the sample
Omitting limitations to appear stronger
Recommending further research with no specifics
checklist: No new material appears here
Each objective is addressed
The contribution is stated in one sentence
Limitations are specific to this design
Future research follows from those limitations
guides.takeaway: Honest limitations make a conclusion stronger, not weaker.
guides.seoTitle: How to write a conclusion and recommendations
guides.metaDescription: Close the study honestly: findings, contribution, limitations and what comes next.

guides.title: How to format references in APA 7th Edition
guides.description: Cite accurately and format consistently so every source can be traced.
guides.intro: References let a reader verify every claim you made. Formatting is the least of it; accuracy is the point.
guides.whatIsIt: APA 7th Edition governs in-text citation and the reference list: author–date in text, alphabetical entries with a hanging indent, and DOIs given as full links.
guides.whyItMatters: Examiners check that every in-text citation has a matching reference and the reverse. Inaccurate or missing citation is treated as a research-integrity matter, not a formatting slip.

howTo.text: Use a reference manager. Reconstructing citations at the end is where errors and accidental plagiarism enter.
Every citation appears in the list; every entry is cited at least once.
Journal article, book, chapter, website and DOI entries each have a fixed shape. Apply it consistently.
Given as https://doi.org/ followed by the identifier. Never invent or guess one.

howTo.step: Verify every entry you did not read
howTo.text: Never copy a reference from another paper's list without checking the original.
Some universities mandate a specific edition or a local variant. Check before formatting.

examples.strong: Formatting template only: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of the article in sentence case. Journal Name, Volume(Issue), 00–00. https://doi.org/xx.xxxx/xxxxxx
examples.weak: Formatting template only: Author, A. (n.d.). Some article. Retrieved from a website.

mistakes: Citations in the text that never appear in the reference list
Inconsistent formatting across entries
Copying a reference from another paper without checking it
Inventing or guessing a DOI
checklist: Every in-text citation has a matching entry
Entries are alphabetical with a hanging indent
DOIs are full https://doi.org/ links
No entry was copied unverified from another source
The edition matches my institution's requirement
guides.takeaway: The reference list is a verification tool. Accuracy matters more than neatness.
guides.seoTitle: How to format references in APA 7th Edition
guides.metaDescription: Cite accurately and format consistently so every source can be traced.

guides.title: How to format, proofread and submit a thesis
guides.description: Meet your university's requirements exactly and submit without avoidable delay.
guides.intro: Submission is a compliance task. Most delays are formatting failures, not academic ones.
guides.whatIsIt: Final submission covers formatting to the university template, proofreading, the similarity check, required front and back matter, approvals, and the submission itself.
guides.whyItMatters: Universities return submissions for margin widths, missing certificates and incorrect declarations. These are entirely avoidable with a checklist and some time.

howTo.text: Margins, fonts, spacing, pagination and heading levels come from your university, not from convention.
Title page, declaration, certificates, acknowledgements, contents, lists of tables and figures, appendices.
One pass for structure, one for language, one for figures and tables, one for references. Not all at once.

Read the matched sources rather than the percentage. A single uncited paragraph matters more than a high total drawn from quotations and the reference list. Where text matches, cite it properly — never reword to reduce a score.
Supervisor sign-off and any departmental clearance, with time allowed for revisions.
Portals close on time and fail under load. Do not submit on the final evening.

examples.strong: Example only: a similarity report consisting entirely of correctly quoted material, standard method phrasing and the reference list.
examples.weak: Example only: replacing words with synonyms while keeping the source's sentence structure, in order to reduce a similarity score.

mistakes: Leaving formatting to the final week
Treating the similarity percentage as the only thing that matters
Rewording matched text instead of citing it properly
Submitting without departmental approval in hand
checklist: The document follows the official template exactly
All required certificates and declarations are included
Proofreading was done in separate passes
The similarity report was read source by source
Approvals are collected and the deadline is not tonight
guides.takeaway: Read the matched sources, not the percentage — and cite rather than reword.
guides.seoTitle: How to format, proofread and submit a thesis
guides.metaDescription: Meet your university's requirements exactly and submit without avoidable delay.

guides.title: How to select a research problem for a paper
guides.description: Choose a problem narrow enough for a single paper and supported by recent literature.
guides.intro: A paper answers one question well. A thesis can answer several; a paper cannot.
guides.whatIsIt: A paper-scale research problem is a single, specific question a reader of your target journal would recognise as open, and which your available evidence can address.
guides.whyItMatters: Most desk rejections are scope problems, not quality problems. A problem sized for a thesis, submitted as a paper, reads as unfocused however well it is written.

howTo.step: Start from what you already have
howTo.text: Existing data, a completed chapter, or a finding that surprised you.
Read the last two years of your target journals. A problem nobody is discussing is hard to place.
If you need the word “and” twice to state it, it is probably two papers.
You need enough to support a claim, not merely enough to describe something.

howTo.step: Write the contribution in one sentence
howTo.text: If you cannot, the problem is not yet defined.

examples.strong: Example only: whether a specific well-established measure behaves consistently in a population where it has not previously been validated.
examples.weak: Example only: an examination of everything currently known about a broad field.

mistakes: Submitting a thesis-sized problem as a single paper
Choosing a question with no recent discussion in the field
Defining the problem after the analysis, to fit the result
Being unable to state the contribution in one sentence
checklist: The problem is one question, not several
Recent literature shows it is still open
My evidence is sufficient to support a claim
I can state the contribution in one sentence
The problem fits a journal I have actually read
guides.takeaway: One question, answered well, beats three questions answered partially.
guides.seoTitle: How to select a research problem for a paper
guides.metaDescription: Choose a problem narrow enough for a single paper and supported by recent literature.

guides.title: How to write a literature review for a research paper
guides.description: Write a compact review that positions your contribution rather than surveying a field.
guides.intro: A paper's review is an argument compressed into a few paragraphs, not a chapter.
guides.whatIsIt: In a paper, the review establishes what is known, identifies the specific opening your study addresses, and stops. Space is limited, so every citation must earn its place.
guides.whyItMatters: Reviewers read the review to decide whether you know the field and whether your claim is genuinely new. A survey that does not position your work signals neither.

howTo.text: Review only what a reader needs to understand your contribution.
Two or three themes, each ending with what remains unresolved.

howTo.step: Cite the recent and the foundational
howTo.text: Reviewers notice when the last three years are missing.
One or two sentences connecting the review directly to your objectives.
Summarise in your own words and cite. Never reuse a source's sentence structure with words substituted.

examples.strong: Example only: two themes are summarised in six sentences each, and the paragraph closes by naming the population where the measure has not been tested.
examples.weak: Example only: twenty studies summarised one after another, with no synthesis.

mistakes: Reviewing the whole field instead of what the paper needs
Omitting recent work reviewers will expect to see
Listing studies without grouping or comparison
Close paraphrasing that keeps the source's phrasing
checklist: The review only covers what my contribution needs
Sources are grouped by theme or disagreement
Recent and foundational work are both present
The opening my study addresses is named explicitly
Every summary is in my own words and cited
guides.takeaway: Review what your argument needs. Everything else belongs in a different paper.
guides.seoTitle: How to write a literature review for a research paper
guides.metaDescription: Write a compact review that positions your contribution rather than surveying a field.

guides.title: How to write research objectives for a paper
guides.description: State a focused aim and objectives a reviewer can match to your results.
guides.intro: In a paper, objectives are often a single paragraph — which makes precision more important, not less.
guides.whatIsIt: Paper objectives state what the study set out to establish, in terms that map directly onto the results you will report.
guides.whyItMatters: Reviewers check whether your results answer your stated objectives. Any mismatch reads as either over-claiming or a missing analysis.

howTo.step: State the aim in one sentence
howTo.text: Placed at the end of the introduction.
More than three is usually a sign the paper is carrying too much.
Compare, estimate, test, characterise — each tied to something you actually did.
Say what the paper adds, without overstating it.
Every objective must have a corresponding result, and every result an objective.

examples.strong: Example only — objective: to test whether a measure retains its factor structure in a population where it has not previously been validated.
examples.weak: Example only — objective: to explore various aspects of the subject.

mistakes: More objectives than the paper can support
Objectives that no reported result addresses
Results reported that answer no stated objective
Verbs describing work the analysis never performed
checklist: The aim is one sentence
There are no more than three objectives
Each verb matches something I actually did
Every objective has a corresponding result
No result is orphaned from an objective
guides.takeaway: Objectives and results must map one to one. Reviewers check.
guides.seoTitle: How to write research objectives for a paper
guides.metaDescription: State a focused aim and objectives a reviewer can match to your results.

guides.title: How to write the methodology section of a paper
guides.description: Give enough detail for replication, in the space a journal allows.
guides.intro: A paper's method section is written for replication, compressed to journal length.
guides.whatIsIt: It states design, participants or materials, procedure, measures and analysis — enough that a competent reader in your field could repeat the study.
guides.whyItMatters: Insufficient methodological detail is among the most common reasons for major revisions. Reviewers cannot evaluate what you do not describe.

howTo.text: Many specify subheadings. Use theirs, not a generic template.
Selection, size, and relevant characteristics.
What happened, in what sequence, with what instrument.
Source, scoring, and reliability evidence in your sample.

howTo.step: Name the analysis and its assumptions
howTo.text: Including software where convention requires it.
Committee, approval reference and consent procedure.

examples.strong: Example only: the sampling frame, response rate, instrument source and reliability in this sample are each reported in two sentences.
examples.weak: Example only: a standard questionnaire was distributed and analysed statistically.

mistakes: Omitting detail a reader would need to replicate the study
Using a generic template instead of the journal's structure
Reporting an instrument without reliability evidence
Leaving out ethics approval where it was required
checklist: A competent reader could repeat this study
The journal's own structure is followed
Measures carry reliability evidence from my sample
The analysis plan and its assumptions are stated
Ethics approval and consent are reported
guides.takeaway: Write the method for someone who intends to repeat it.
guides.seoTitle: How to write the methodology section of a paper
guides.metaDescription: Give enough detail for replication, in the space a journal allows.

guides.title: How to analyse evidence for a research paper
guides.description: Analyse transparently and report what you actually did, including what did not work.
guides.intro: The analysis you report must be the analysis you performed.
guides.whatIsIt: This covers preparation, the analytic procedure, assumption checks, and honest reporting of everything the analysis produced.
guides.whyItMatters: Selective reporting — showing only the analyses that worked — is a research-integrity failure, not a presentational choice. Journals increasingly ask for analysis plans.

howTo.text: Cleaning, exclusions and transformations, each with a reason.
Report the checks, not just the results.
Deviations are acceptable when disclosed; undisclosed ones are not.
Including non-significant and unexpected results.
Exact statistics, effect sizes and, where appropriate, the data or code.

examples.strong: Example only: the pre-planned test was reported alongside a sensitivity check, and the non-significant secondary outcome was reported in full.
examples.weak: Example only: only the analyses that produced significant results were reported.

mistakes: Reporting only the analyses that worked
Trying tests until one reaches significance
Omitting assumption checks
Adjusting or excluding data to obtain an expected result
checklist: Preparation and exclusions are documented
Assumption checks are reported
Deviations from the plan are disclosed
Non-significant results are included
Statistics are reported precisely enough to verify
guides.takeaway: Report the analysis you ran, including the parts that did not work.
guides.seoTitle: How to analyse evidence for a research paper
guides.metaDescription: Analyse transparently and report what you actually did, including what did not work.

guides.title: How to write a research manuscript
guides.description: Structure a manuscript reviewers can follow and editors can process.
guides.intro: A manuscript is a structured argument, not an essay about your study.
guides.whatIsIt: Most empirical papers follow introduction, method, results and discussion, with an abstract that summarises all four and a conclusion that closes the argument.
guides.whyItMatters: Editors screen for structure and fit before quality. A manuscript that does not follow the expected shape is harder to review and easier to reject.

howTo.text: Method and results are the most factual and the easiest to write.

howTo.step: Write the introduction to set up the contribution
howTo.text: Broad context, narrowing to the specific opening, ending with your objectives.
It must summarise what the paper actually says, not what you hoped it would.
Results report; discussion interprets.

howTo.step: Cut to the word limit honestly
howTo.text: Remove material, do not compress sentences until they are unreadable.
A day away reveals problems no amount of rereading on the day will.

examples.strong: Example only: an abstract stating the problem, method, principal result and implication, in four sentences.
examples.weak: Example only: an abstract describing what the paper will discuss, without stating any finding.

mistakes: Writing the abstract before the paper is finished
Merging results and discussion
Exceeding the word limit and cutting content arbitrarily at the end
An introduction that never states the contribution
checklist: The structure matches the journal's expectations
The abstract reflects what the paper actually found
Results and discussion are separate
The word limit is met by removing material, not compressing prose
The introduction ends with clear objectives
guides.takeaway: Write the middle first and the abstract last.
guides.seoTitle: How to write a research manuscript
guides.metaDescription: Structure a manuscript reviewers can follow and editors can process.

guides.title: How to prepare tables, figures and references
guides.description: Present evidence so it can be read, checked and reused without the surrounding text.
guides.intro: A good table or figure is comprehensible on its own.
guides.whatIsIt: This covers table and figure design, captions, numbering, accessibility, and a complete reference list in the journal's required style.
guides.whyItMatters: Production teams return manuscripts for inconsistent numbering, missing permissions and unreadable figures. These delays are avoidable.

howTo.text: A table for precise values, a figure for pattern or relationship. Never both for the same data.
The caption and labels should explain it without the body text.
Resolution, file format, colour policy and numbering.

howTo.step: Do not rely on colour alone
howTo.text: Use shape, pattern or direct labels as well, so the figure survives greyscale and colour-vision differences.
Any reproduced figure needs permission and attribution.
Verify against the original. Never copy an entry from another paper's list.

examples.strong: Example only: a figure whose caption states the sample, the measure and the comparison, with series distinguished by both pattern and label.
examples.weak: Example only: a chart labelled “Results” with series distinguished only by colour.

mistakes: Presenting the same data as both a table and a figure
Captions that cannot be understood without the body text
Relying on colour alone to distinguish series
Reusing a published figure without permission
checklist: Each table or figure can be read on its own
The journal's specification is met
No meaning depends on colour alone
Permissions are cleared for reproduced material
Every reference was verified against the original
guides.takeaway: If a reader must consult the text to understand your figure, redesign the figure.
guides.seoTitle: How to prepare tables, figures and references
guides.metaDescription: Present evidence so it can be read, checked and reused without the surrounding text.

guides.title: How to select a journal for your research paper
guides.description: Match your paper to a journal's scope, and verify every claim a journal makes about itself.
guides.intro: Journal selection is a scope-matching exercise, plus verification.
guides.whatIsIt: Selection means assessing aims and scope, article types, audience, review process, fees and — critically — independently verifying any indexing a journal advertises.
guides.whyItMatters: Scope mismatch causes most desk rejections. Separately, predatory publishing costs scholars money and can render work unusable for degree or promotion purposes.

howTo.step: Read what the journal actually published
howTo.text: The last two years. Would your paper sit comfortably beside them?

howTo.step: Check aims, scope and article type
howTo.text: Many rejections are simply the wrong article type.

Check the database's own published list. A journal's website is not evidence, and delisted journals often continue advertising former status. Never state that a journal is indexed anywhere unless you have verified it independently.

howTo.step: Confirm the editorial board is real
howTo.text: Can you find those people, at those institutions?
Charges revealed only after acceptance are a warning sign.
Publication promised within days means there was no peer review.
Reputable journals do not email strangers asking for manuscripts.

examples.strong: Example only: a shortlist of three journals whose recent issues include comparable study designs, with fees and review timelines confirmed from each journal's own policy pages.
examples.weak: Example only: choosing a journal because an unsolicited email promised rapid publication and listed several database names.

mistakes: Trusting indexing claims made on the journal's own website
Submitting without reading recent issues
Ignoring fees until after acceptance
Responding to unsolicited invitations to submit
checklist: I have read recent issues of the journal
My article type is one the journal publishes
Any indexing claim was verified at the database's source list
The editorial board is verifiable
All fees are known in advance
guides.takeaway: Verify at the source. No consultancy, agent or journal email can substitute for that — and no one can guarantee acceptance.
guides.seoTitle: How to select a journal for your research paper
guides.metaDescription: Match your paper to a journal's scope, and verify every claim a journal makes about itself.

guides.title: How to follow journal author guidelines
guides.description: Meet every formatting and submission requirement before you submit.
guides.intro: Author guidelines are compliance requirements, not suggestions.
guides.whatIsIt: They specify structure, word limits, reference style, figure formats, anonymisation, declarations and the files a submission must contain.
guides.whyItMatters: Editorial offices return non-compliant submissions without review. Each return costs weeks for something that takes an afternoon to fix.

howTo.step: Read the guidelines before the final draft
howTo.text: Reformatting afterwards wastes more time than writing to the specification.
Word limit, structure, reference style, figure format, file types.
Double-blind review means removing identifying details from the manuscript and the file metadata.
Authorship, contributions, funding, conflicts of interest, data availability.
Everyone listed contributed; everyone who contributed is listed. Authorship is never traded, gifted or sold.
Briefly: what the paper shows, why this journal, and confirmation it is not under review elsewhere.

examples.strong: Example only: a submission pack containing an anonymised manuscript, a separate title page, figures at the specified resolution, and completed declarations.
examples.weak: Example only: submitting a manuscript formatted for a different journal.

mistakes: Formatting for one journal and submitting to another
Missing declarations, which delay the submission
Failing to anonymise for double-blind review
Adding an author who did not contribute
checklist: The manuscript follows this journal's guidelines exactly
Word limit and reference style are met
Files are anonymised where required
All declarations are complete
Every listed author has contributed and approved
guides.takeaway: An afternoon spent on the guidelines saves weeks in the editorial office.
guides.seoTitle: How to follow journal author guidelines
guides.metaDescription: Meet every formatting and submission requirement before you submit.

guides.title: How to submit and respond to reviewer comments
guides.description: Understand the review process and answer reviewers with evidence rather than defensiveness.
guides.intro: Major revisions are a normal, often positive outcome — not a failure.
guides.whatIsIt: Submission passes through editorial screening, peer review, a decision, revision and resubmission. Editors and reviewers decide; nobody else can.
guides.whyItMatters: Scholars often read a critical review as rejection. Understanding the stages, and responding point by point with evidence, materially improves the outcome — though it never guarantees it.

howTo.text: Many rejections happen here, on scope, before review begins.
Genuine peer review takes weeks at minimum, usually months.
Once for the emotion, once for the substance. Respond to the second reading.
Quote each comment, state what you changed, and give the page or line.
You may decline a change if you justify it courteously and substantively.
Late resubmission may be treated as a new submission.

examples.strong: Example only: a response table quoting each comment, describing the change made, and citing the revised page — including one courteous, evidenced disagreement.
examples.weak: Example only: a reply stating that the reviewer has misunderstood the paper, with no supporting explanation.

mistakes: Treating major revisions as a rejection
Responding to reviewers defensively rather than with evidence
Making changes without documenting them in the response
Submitting the same manuscript to several journals at once
checklist: I understand which stage my manuscript is at
Every comment has a documented response
Changes cite the revised page or line
Disagreements are justified, not dismissive
The paper is under review at one journal only
guides.takeaway: Answer every comment with evidence. Acceptance is the editor's decision, and nobody can promise it.
guides.seoTitle: How to submit and respond to reviewer comments
guides.metaDescription: Understand the review process and answer reviewers with evidence rather than defensiveness.
